results.question: Do creatures phasing back in trigger enter the battlefield abilities?
results.text:
No, creatures phasing back in do not trigger "enters the battlefield" abilities. Phasing in is not a zone change; the permanent is treated as though it never left the battlefield. Therefore, abilities that trigger when a permanent enters the battlefield do not trigger when it phases in.

This is because phasing does not cause a permanent to change zones. Rule [702.26d] states that the phasing event does not cause a permanent to change zones or control, and zone-change triggers (which include enters-the-battlefield triggers) do not trigger when a permanent phases in or out. Rule [603.6a] defines enters-the-battlefield triggers as zone-change triggers that occur when a permanent enters the battlefield from another zone. Since phasing in is not entering the battlefield from another zone, these abilities do not trigger.

For clarity: "Phasing in" means a permanent's status changes from "phased out" to "phased in," and the game once again treats it as though it exists on the battlefield (rule [702.26c]). It was never in another zone like the exile zone or the graveyard.

results.question: how does trample work with deathtouch?
results.text:
A creature with both trample and deathtouch only needs to assign 1 damage to each creature blocking it before it can assign the rest of its damage to the defending player, planeswalker, or battle. This is because any nonzero amount of damage from a source with deathtouch is considered lethal damage for the purpose of determining excess damage.

Specifically, when assigning combat damage for an attacking creature with trample, its controller must first assign lethal damage to all creatures blocking it before any excess can be assigned to the player, planeswalker, or battle it's attacking. Rule 702.2c states that any nonzero amount of combat damage assigned to a creature by a source with deathtouch is considered lethal damage for determining excess. Therefore, for each blocking creature, assigning 1 damage is sufficient to count as lethal damage, regardless of that blocking creature's toughness. Once 1 damage has been assigned to each blocking creature, all remaining damage from the attacking creature with trample and deathtouch can be assigned as its controller chooses among those blocking creatures and the defending player, planeswalker, or battle. This interaction is also referenced in rule 120.4a, which notes that any amount of damage greater than 1 is excess damage if the source dealing that damage to a creature has deathtouch.

results.question: is storm a triggered ability that can be countered?
results.text: Yes, Storm is a triggered ability that can be countered by effects that specifically counter abilities. Storm is a triggered ability that functions on the stack [702.40a]. Triggered abilities on the stack are not spells, so they cannot be countered by effects that counter only spells, but they can be countered by effects that specifically counter abilities [113.9]. Therefore, an effect like Stifle or Tale's End, which counters target activated or triggered ability, can counter a Storm ability on the stack, preventing the copies from being created.

results.question: can i use cards with hybrid mana symbols in a commander deck that only has one of those colors?
results.text:
No, you cannot use a card with a hybrid mana symbol in a Commander deck if your commander's color identity includes only one of the symbol's colors. For example, a card with a {G/W} hybrid mana symbol cannot be in a mono-green or mono-white Commander deck.

This is because a card's color identity is determined by the colors of all mana symbols in its mana cost and rules text [903.4]. A hybrid mana symbol like {G/W} is both of its component colors (green and white) [202.2d, 107.4e]. Therefore, a card containing a {G/W} symbol has a color identity that includes both green and white. Commander deck construction rules require that every color in a card's color identity must also be found in the color identity of the deck's commander [903.5c]. If your commander's color identity is only green (or only white), it does not include both colors of the hybrid symbol, so the card is illegal for that deck.

The answer is based on the provided rules for two-player Commander. The same deck construction rules apply in multiplayer Commander games.

results.question: can I respond to the untap step?
results.text:
No, you cannot respond to the untap step. No player receives priority during the untap step, so no spells can be cast and no abilities can be activated [502.4]. The untap step ends automatically once its turn-based actions (like untapping permanents) are completed, without any player getting priority [500.3, 117.3a].

This answer is for the two-player case. The rules provided do not specify any differences for multiplayer games regarding priority during the untap step, so the same restriction applies regardless of the number of players.

results.question: are creatures still considered attacking creatures during the end of combat step?
results.text:
Yes, creatures are still considered attacking creatures during the end of combat step. They are removed from combat only when the end of combat step ends, which is when the combat phase ends and the postcombat main phase begins.

According to the rules, a creature remains an attacking creature until it is removed from combat or the combat phase ends, whichever comes first [Attacking Creature, 508.1k, 508.4]. The combat phase ends when the end of combat step ends [511.3]. Therefore, for the entire duration of the end of combat step, creatures that were declared as attackers or put onto the battlefield attacking are still attacking creatures. They are removed from combat as a turn-based action as soon as the end of combat step ends, marking the transition to the postcombat main phase [511.3].

results.question: Do you cast lands?
results.text:
No, you do not cast lands. You play lands as a special action that does not use the stack.

According to the rules, playing a land is a special action distinct from casting a spell [305.1, 505.6b, 701.18a]. A land card is played by putting it onto the battlefield from your hand when you have priority, during your main phase, and when the stack is empty. This action does not use the stack, is not a spell, and cannot be responded to with instants or activated abilities.

Rule 305.9 and rule 300.2a explicitly state that an object that is both a land and another card type (like an artifact land) can only be played as a land and cannot be cast as a spell. Furthermore, rule 202.1b notes that lands have no mana cost and are played without paying any costs.

The term "play" encompasses both playing a land and casting a spell, depending on the card type [601.1a, 701.18b]. Therefore, for a land card, the appropriate action is to play it, not to cast it.

results.question: can I sacrifice an evoked creature before that creature's evoke triggered ability resolves?
results.text:
No, you cannot sacrifice an evoked creature before its own evoke triggered ability resolves, because the sacrifice is a consequence of that ability resolving and you do not get priority to take actions while it is on the stack.

An evoked creature has the triggered ability: "When this permanent enters, if its evoke cost was paid, its controller sacrifices it." This ability triggers when the creature enters the battlefield and is put on the stack the next time a player would receive priority [603.3d]. Once this triggered ability is on the stack, players must pass priority for it to resolve [608.1]. You cannot take a special action like sacrificing a creature (unless a card like Circling Vultures specifically allows it) while a spell or ability is waiting to resolve, because you only get priority after it resolves or after another spell/ability is put on the stack. The sacrifice from evoke is not an action you can take at will; it is the result of the triggered ability resolving. Therefore, you cannot preemptively sacrifice the evoked creature to something else before its own evoke trigger resolves.

If the question is about sacrificing the evoked creature to a different triggered ability that also triggered when it entered (like an exploit ability), those abilities would all be put on the stack before any player gets priority [603.3d]. You could order them so the exploit trigger resolves first, allowing you to sacrifice the evoked creature. In that case, the evoke trigger would still be on the stack and would resolve afterward. However, if the evoke trigger's condition ("if its evoke cost was paid") is still true, it will try to make you sacrifice the evoked creature. Since the evoked creature is already sacrificed, the evoke trigger's instruction becomes impossible to fully carry out, but the ability will still resolve. The source of the ability (the evoked creature) uses its last known information if needed [113.7a].

This answer assumes a two-player game, as the provided rules do not specify multiplayer interactions.

Cited rules: [702.74a] defines evoke and its triggered ability. [603.3d] explains that triggered abilities are put on the stack the next time a player would get priority. [603.12] and [113.7a] are cited for context on reflexive triggers and source information, though the core answer relies on the timing of priority and the nature of the evoke trigger.

results.question: if a card loses all abilities, does that include keyword abilities?
results.text:
Yes, if a card loses all abilities, that includes keyword abilities. Keyword abilities are abilities, so an effect that removes all abilities removes them as well.

According to rule 113.10, effects can remove abilities of objects, and an effect that removes an ability states that the object 'loses' that ability. Rule 113.10b clarifies that effects that remove an ability remove all instances of it. Rule 702.1 defines keyword abilities as abilities that are summarized by a keyword on the card. Therefore, a 'lose all abilities' effect applies to keyword abilities just as it does to any other ability written out in full. The effect removes all abilities the object has, regardless of whether they are expressed as keywords or as full rules text.

results.question: can i draw cards if i'm already at my maximum hand size?
results.text:
Yes, you can draw cards even if you are already at your maximum hand size. A player's maximum hand size only imposes a limit during the cleanup step, where you must discard down to that number; it does not prevent you from drawing cards at other times.

Rule 402.2 states that a player may have any number of cards in their hand, but as part of their cleanup step, they must discard excess cards down to the maximum hand size. This means drawing cards is always possible, regardless of current hand size. The restriction only applies as a turn-based action during the cleanup step, as detailed in rules 514.1 and 703.4n.

results.question: what happens when a planeswalker has 0 or less loyalty counters?
results.text:
A planeswalker with 0 loyalty counters is put into its owner's graveyard as a state-based action. This happens automatically and doesn't use the stack.

According to the rules, a planeswalker's loyalty is equal to the number of loyalty counters on it [122.1e, 306.5c]. Rule 306.9 states: "If a planeswalker’s loyalty is 0, it’s put into its owner’s graveyard. (This is a state-based action. See rule 704.)" This is reiterated in rule 704.5i, which lists the state-based action: "If a planeswalker has loyalty 0, it’s put into its owner’s graveyard." State-based actions are checked whenever a player would receive priority and do not use the stack [704.1]. The phrase "0 or less" in the question is functionally the same as "0" for this purpose, as a planeswalker cannot have a negative number of loyalty counters; if damage or an effect would remove more counters than are present, the planeswalker simply goes to zero loyalty and is put into the graveyard.

results.question: do non-creature artifacts die?
results.text:
No, non-creature artifacts do not die. The term "dies" is defined specifically as a creature or planeswalker being put into a graveyard from the battlefield [Dies, 700.4]. Since a non-creature artifact is not a creature or a planeswalker, its movement from the battlefield to a graveyard is not a death event, regardless of the cause (such as being destroyed, sacrificed, or having its toughness reduced to 0).

Reasoning: The definition of "dies" is exclusive to creatures and planeswalkers. The rules context does not provide any exception that would extend this term to other permanent types like artifacts, enchantments, or battles. Therefore, when a non-creature artifact is put into a graveyard from the battlefield, it is not considered to have died.

results.question: what happens if i should draw a card when my library is empty?
results.text:
If you attempt to draw a card from an empty library, you lose the game the next time a player would receive priority. This is a state-based action. [121.4, 704.5b]

Specifically, rule 121.4 states that a player who attempts to draw a card from a library with no cards in it loses the game the next time a player would receive priority. Rule 704.5b lists this as a state-based action, meaning it is checked automatically and doesn't use the stack. The loss occurs even if the draw is part of a choice offered by an effect, as rule 121.3 clarifies you can choose to draw even with an empty library. If an effect would have you draw more cards than are in your library, you draw the remaining cards and then lose the game the next time state-based actions are checked. [104.3c]

results.question: what are the steps in combat and when do I have priority as the defending player?
results.text:
The combat phase has five steps in order: beginning of combat, declare attackers, declare blockers, combat damage, and end of combat. As the defending player, you receive priority for the first time in the combat phase after the active player passes priority during the beginning of combat step, and again after the active player passes priority in each subsequent step where players get priority.

According to rule [506.1], the combat phase consists of the beginning of combat, declare attackers, declare blockers, combat damage, and end of combat steps. The declare blockers and combat damage steps are skipped if no creatures attack. Rule [117.3a] states that the active player receives priority at the beginning of most steps, after any turn-based actions and triggered abilities are handled. This means at the start of the beginning of combat step, the active player gets priority first. As the defending player, you will get priority only after the active player passes it to you. This pattern repeats in the declare attackers, declare blockers, and end of combat steps. In the combat damage step, rule [510.2] specifies that no player has priority between damage assignment and damage being dealt; however, players do get priority after damage is dealt and before the step ends, with the active player receiving it first. The provided rules are framed for a two-player game, where rule [506.2] defines the nonactive player as the defending player. In a multiplayer game using the 'Attack Multiple Players' option (rule [802.2]), all opponents are defending players, but the priority sequence remains the same: the active player (attacking player) gets priority first in each step.

results.question: can i respond to a mana ability?
results.text:
No, you cannot respond to a mana ability. Mana abilities resolve immediately and do not use the stack, so there is no opportunity for players to cast spells or activate abilities in response to them.

A mana ability is an activated or triggered ability that could create mana and does not use the stack [Mana Ability]. Activated mana abilities do not go on the stack and resolve immediately after they are activated, so they cannot be targeted, countered, or otherwise responded to [605.3b]. Triggered mana abilities also do not go on the stack and resolve immediately after the mana ability that triggered them, without waiting for priority [605.4a]. The general rule for mana abilities is that they do not use the stack, and a player can activate them even if they don't have priority under certain circumstances [113.4]. If a player had priority before a mana ability was activated, that player gets priority after it resolves [405.6c], but the mana ability itself cannot be responded to.

results.question: can I respond to a cost being paid?
results.text:
No, you cannot respond to a cost being paid. Paying a cost is a single, atomic action that does not use the stack and during which no player receives priority.

This is because paying a cost is part of the process of casting a spell, activating an ability, or taking a special action, and is not itself a separate action that uses the stack. According to rule 118.1, to pay a cost, a player carries out the instructions specified by the spell, ability, or effect. Rule 118.2 states that if a cost includes a mana payment, the player paying the cost has a chance to activate mana abilities before paying, but the payment itself is not interruptible. The steps for casting a spell in rules 601.2g and 601.2h show that determining and paying the total cost are sequential steps performed by the casting player without passing priority. Rule 118.10 clarifies that each payment applies to only one spell or ability, and rule 602.4 states that activating an ability that alters costs won't affect spells and abilities already on the stack, which implies cost determination and payment are complete before the object is fully on the stack and open to responses. Furthermore, rule 608.2g indicates that during the resolution of a spell or ability, no other spells can normally be cast and no other abilities can normally be activated, which includes the moment a cost is being paid as part of that resolution if a spell is being cast during resolution.

Therefore, once a player begins to pay a cost, they must complete the payment in full (rule 601.2h states partial payments are not allowed) without any other player having the opportunity to take actions in response to individual components of the payment.

results.question: can you explain layers?
results.text:
Yes, layers are a system used to determine the order in which continuous effects are applied to an object's characteristics. The game applies all applicable continuous effects in a series of layers, from 1 to 7, with some layers having sublayers. This ensures a consistent final state for an object's power, toughness, color, type, abilities, and other characteristics.

First, you start with the object's actual printed characteristics (or the characteristics defined for a token or copy). Then, continuous effects are applied in this order: Layer 1 modifies copiable values (like copy effects). Layer 2 applies control-changing effects. Layer 3 applies text-changing effects. Layer 4 applies type-changing effects. Layer 5 applies color-changing effects. Layer 6 applies ability-adding or -removing effects. Finally, Layer 7 applies power- and toughness-changing effects, which itself has sublayers: 7a for characteristic-defining abilities that set P/T, 7b for effects that set power and/or toughness to specific numbers, and 7c for effects that modify power and/or toughness (like +1/+1).

Within a layer or sublayer, effects are usually applied in timestamp order (earlier before later), but dependency can override this order. An effect depends on another if applying the other effect would change what the first effect applies to or what it does. A single effect with multiple parts applies each part in its appropriate layer. The values determined after applying all effects in Layer 1 become the object's copiable values for purposes of copying.

For example, if an effect makes a creature white (Layer 5) and another gives white creatures +1/+1 (Layer 7c), the creature gets the bonus. If an effect later changes its color to red, the bonus stops applying. The system ensures all effects interact predictably.

results.question: how does the legend rule work?
results.text:
The legend rule is a state-based action that causes a player who controls two or more legendary permanents with the same name to put all but one of them into their owners' graveyards. Specifically, when a player controls two or more legendary permanents with the exact same name, that player chooses one of them to keep, and the rest are put into their owners' graveyards. This action happens automatically and does not use the stack.

This rule applies to any permanent with the legendary supertype, which includes legendary creatures, legendary enchantments, legendary artifacts, legendary lands, and planeswalkers (as planeswalker cards now have the legendary supertype). The rule only cares about the exact name of the permanent; legendary permanents with different names can coexist under the same player's control without issue. The legend rule is checked, along with all other state-based actions, each time a player would receive priority.

results.question: when does my creature die after its been marked with a lethal amount of damage?
results.text:
A creature with lethal damage marked on it is destroyed the next time state-based actions are checked, which happens immediately before any player would get priority. This means the creature dies instantly when the game checks, not at the end of a phase or step.

Specifically, state-based actions are checked whenever a player would get priority [704.3], [117.5]. The condition for destruction is: if a creature has toughness greater than 0, has damage marked on it, and the total damage marked is greater than or equal to its toughness, that creature is destroyed [704.5g]. Damage remains marked on a creature until it regenerates or the cleanup step [120.6], [302.7].

For example, if your 2/2 creature is dealt 2 damage by Lightning Bolt, state-based actions are checked after Lightning Bolt finishes resolving and before any player gets priority. The game sees the 2/2 creature has 2 damage marked (equal to its toughness) and destroys it immediately. There is no window to activate abilities or cast spells to save it between the damage being dealt and the state-based action check that destroys it, unless an effect explicitly creates such a window (like an ability that triggers from the damage being dealt).

If the turn or combat phase is ended by an effect (like Mandate of Peace), state-based actions are also checked as part of that process [724.1c], [724.2c], which would destroy the creature at that moment.

In the cleanup step, damage is removed [514.2], but if a creature has lethal damage when the cleanup step begins, state-based actions are checked at the start of the cleanup step (before damage is removed) and would destroy the creature then [514.3a], [704.3].

results.question: can I cast my commander from exile?
results.text:
Yes, you can cast your commander from exile, but only if a rule or effect specifically allows you to cast spells from exile and you are allowed to look at the card if it is exiled face down. The commander designation is retained in exile, and there is no general rule that prohibits casting a commander from that zone. However, you must have a specific permission to cast a spell from exile, such as from an ability like that of "Oblivion Ring."

Your commander is a card designated as a commander, and this attribute is retained in all zones, including exile [903.3d]. The rules for commanders also state that effects referring to a characteristic of "your commander" can find it and see its current characteristics in all zones, including exile [903.3e]. This confirms the commander is a recognizable object in exile.

The general rule for casting spells states a player can begin to cast a spell only if a rule or effect allows that player to cast it and no rule or effect prohibits it [601.3f]. There is no rule in the provided context that prohibits casting a commander from exile. However, to cast a spell from exile, you must have a specific permission from another source (like a spell or ability) that says you may cast it from exile. For example, if your commander is exiled by "Oblivion Ring," you could cast it when the "Oblivion Ring" leaves the battlefield if that effect allows it.

Additionally, if the commander is exiled face down, you may cast it only if you are allowed to look at the face-down card in exile and the resulting spell has the qualities specified by the effect allowing you to cast it [406.3b], [601.3f].

Note that the commander's ability to return to the command zone from exile is a state-based action [903.9a], but choosing to leave it in exile does not prevent you from later casting it if an effect allows you to do so.

results.question: what happens during the cleanup step?
results.text:
During the cleanup step, three things happen in order: first, the active player discards down to their maximum hand size if necessary; second, all damage is removed from permanents and all 'until end of turn' and 'this turn' effects end simultaneously; and third, the step normally ends with no player getting priority. However, if after these actions any state-based actions would be performed or any triggered abilities are waiting to be put onto the stack, those are handled and then the active player gets priority, leading to another cleanup step.

Specifically, according to the rules, the cleanup step is part of the ending phase [Cleanup Step]. The step begins with a turn-based action: if the active player's hand contains more cards than their maximum hand size, they discard enough cards to reduce their hand size to that number [514.1]. Next, another turn-based action happens simultaneously: all damage marked on permanents is removed and all 'until end of turn' and 'this turn' effects end [514.2, 703.4p]. Normally, no player receives priority during the cleanup step, so no spells can be cast and no abilities can be activated, and the step ends when these actions are completed [514.3, 500.3].

The exception is detailed in rule 514.3a. After the turn-based actions, the game checks for state-based actions and triggered abilities waiting to be put on the stack (including those that trigger 'at the beginning of the next cleanup step'). If any are found, those state-based actions are performed, then those triggered abilities are put on the stack, then the active player gets priority. Players may then cast spells and activate abilities. Once the stack is empty and all players pass in succession, another cleanup step begins [514.3a]. This process of checking and potentially granting priority can repeat until a cleanup step occurs where no state-based actions are performed and no triggered abilities are waiting, at which point the step ends with no player getting priority [500.3, 514.3a].

results.question: when are state-based actions checked?
results.text:
State-based actions are checked whenever a player would get priority, and also at specific moments when no player gets priority. Specifically, they are checked: 1) Each time a player would get priority, the game first performs all applicable state-based actions as a single event, repeating this process until none are performed [704.3, 117.5]. 2) During the cleanup step, the game checks for state-based actions at the point described in rule 514.3a [514.3a]. 3) When an effect ends the combat phase or ends the turn, state-based actions are checked as part of that process, and no player gets priority afterward [724.2c, 724.1c]. 4) At the beginning of a step or phase, after any turn-based actions are dealt with but before state-based actions are checked and before players receive priority [703.3].

State-based actions are automatic game actions that do not use the stack and are not controlled by any player [704.1, 704.2]. The check is performed repeatedly until no more state-based actions are performed and no triggered abilities are waiting to be put on the stack, at which point the appropriate player gets priority or the step/phase proceeds [704.3, 117.5].

results.question: when can I concede a game?
results.text: You can concede a game at any time. This is a fundamental rule of Magic: The Gathering that cannot be overridden by any card or effect. [104.3a] states a player can concede the game at any time, and that player leaves the game immediately and loses. [405.6g] reiterates that conceding does not use the stack and can be done at any time. [101.1] explicitly notes that the only exception to the rule that card text overrides game rules is that a player can concede the game at any time. This right is absolute, even if you are being controlled by another player, as confirmed by [723.6]. The answer is the same for any number of players, though in team variants like Two-Headed Giant, a player conceding causes their entire team to lose.

results.question: how do I know who the active player is?
results.text:
The active player is the player whose turn it is [Active Player], [102.1].

This definition is fundamental: at any moment, exactly one player is the active player. The rules provided are for a standard game; in a multiplayer game using the shared team turns option, the active team is the team whose turn it is [805.4a], but the concept of a single active player still applies within that structure for certain choices [805.9]. For the purposes of this question based on the provided rules, the active player is simply the one currently taking their turn.

results.question: when someone other than the active player casts a spell, who gets priority first?
results.text:
After a player other than the active player casts a spell, the player who cast the spell gets priority first. This is because the player who cast the spell had priority when they cast it, and rule 117.3c states that if a player has priority when they cast a spell, that player receives priority afterward. Therefore, the non-active player who just cast the spell retains priority and can immediately cast another spell or activate an ability before the active player gets a chance to respond.

This answer is based on the provided rules for a two-player game. The rules provided do not specify any difference for multiplayer games regarding priority after casting a spell, so the same principle likely applies: the player who cast the spell gets priority first, regardless of turn order. However, the provided context lacks specific multiplayer priority rules, so the answer is framed for the two-player case.

results.question: when the active player cast a spell, who gets priority first?
results.text: After the active player casts a spell, the active player gets priority first. This is directly stated by rule 117.3c: 'If a player has priority when they cast a spell, activate an ability, or take a special action, that player receives priority afterward.' Since the active player had priority to cast the spell, they receive priority again immediately after casting it.

results.question: can I hold priority to cast more spells after I've cast one or more spells?
results.text:
Yes, you can hold priority to cast more spells after you have cast one or more spells. After you finish casting a spell, if you had priority before you began casting it, you receive priority again. This allows you to cast another spell before passing priority to other players.

This is based on rule 117.3c, which states that if a player has priority when they cast a spell, that player receives priority afterward. Rule 601.2i confirms this, stating that if the spell's controller had priority before casting it, they get priority after it becomes cast. Therefore, you can retain priority and cast additional spells in succession, as long as you continue to have priority and do not pass it.

results.question: when are lore counters put on sagas?
results.text:
Lore counters are put on Sagas at two specific times: when the Saga enters the battlefield, and at the beginning of its controller's precombat main phase each turn.

First, when a Saga enters the battlefield, it enters with a certain number of lore counters. For a Saga without read ahead, it enters with exactly one lore counter [714.3a]. For a Saga with read ahead, its controller chooses a number between one and its final chapter number as it enters, and it enters with that many lore counters [714.3b], [702.155b]. These are replacement effects.

Second, as a turn-based action that doesn't use the stack, immediately after a player's precombat main phase begins, that player puts a lore counter on each Saga they control with one or more chapter abilities [505.4], [703.4f], [714.3c]. This happens every turn during that player's main phase.

These are the only times lore counters are placed on Sagas as defined by the provided rules. The provided rules are framed for a two-player game; in a multiplayer game, the turn-based action still occurs for the active player at the beginning of their precombat main phase.

results.question: what is a delayed triggered ability?
results.text: A delayed triggered ability is an ability created by a resolving spell or ability, a replacement effect, or a static ability that allows an action, which is set up to trigger and do something at a later time rather than immediately. It contains a triggering condition using "when," "whenever," or "at." [Delayed Triggered Ability, 603.7, 610.2]. It is created during the resolution of the effect that generates it, and it won't trigger until after it has been created, even if its trigger event occurred just beforehand. [603.7a].

results.question: can non-permanent spells have abilities?
results.text: Yes, non-permanent spells (instant and sorcery spells) can have abilities. Specifically, the text of an instant or sorcery spell is a spell ability, which is an ability that functions while the spell is on the stack and is followed as instructions when the spell resolves. [113.3a] The spell has all the characteristics of its card, including its abilities, while it is on the stack. [405.4] However, abilities of an instant or sorcery spell usually function only while that object is on the stack. [113.6]

results.question: can I use a mana ability when a spell with split-second is on the stack?
results.text: Yes, you can activate a mana ability while a spell with split second is on the stack. The split second ability only prevents players from casting other spells or activating abilities that aren't mana abilities. Mana abilities are explicitly allowed. [702.61a] states that split second means players can't cast other spells or activate abilities that aren't mana abilities. [702.61b] clarifies that players may activate mana abilities while a spell with split second is on the stack. Furthermore, [605.3a] and [117.1d] establish that a player may activate a mana ability whenever they have priority, are casting a spell, or a rule asks for a mana payment, even in the middle of casting or resolving a spell. Since a split second spell is on the stack, players have priority at some point before it resolves (unless it's in the middle of resolving), and the rules for split second specifically permit mana abilities.

results.question: [Counterspell] is on top of the stack targeting my [Divination]. When everyone passes priority, what resolves first, and does Divination still resolve?
results.text: Counterspell resolves first, and Divination does not resolve; it is countered and put into its owner's graveyard. When all players pass priority, the spell or ability on top of the stack resolves [608.1]. Counterspell is on top of the stack targeting Divination, so Counterspell resolves first. When Counterspell resolves, it counters its target spell [701.6a]. To counter a spell means to cancel it, removing it from the stack; it doesn't resolve and none of its effects occur, and the countered spell is put into its owner's graveyard [701.6a]. Therefore, Divination is countered, does not resolve, and is put into its owner's graveyard. If Counterspell had somehow been countered or removed from the stack before resolving, then Divination would be the top object and would resolve when priority is passed, drawing two cards and then being put into its owner's graveyard as the final part of its resolution [608.2n].

results.question: My [Charging Rhino] has trample and is blocked by [Vampire Nighthawk], which has deathtouch. How much combat damage do I have to assign to the blocker before I can trample the rest over to the player?
results.text: You must assign at least 1 damage to Vampire Nighthawk before you can assign any damage to the defending player. Because Vampire Nighthawk has deathtouch, any nonzero amount of combat damage assigned to it by a source with deathtouch is considered lethal damage for the purposes of determining excess damage [702.2c]. However, Charging Rhino does not have deathtouch. Therefore, when assigning Charging Rhino's combat damage, you check for lethal damage using the normal definition: an amount of damage greater than or equal to Vampire Nighthawk's toughness [Lethal Damage]. Vampire Nighthawk has toughness 3, so lethal damage for it is 3 damage. According to the trample rules, you must first assign lethal damage to all blocking creatures before you can assign any excess damage to the player [702.19b]. Since Vampire Nighthawk is the only blocker, you must assign at least 3 damage to it. Rule 120.4a, which discusses excess damage being dealt by a source with deathtouch, does not apply here because the source of the damage (Charging Rhino) does not have deathtouch. Therefore, you must assign 3 damage to Vampire Nighthawk; any remaining damage from Charging Rhino's power of 4 can then be assigned to the defending player.

results.question: I have [Monastery Swiftspear] on the battlefield and I cast [Shardless Agent]. When its cascade ability puts a noncreature spell onto the stack, does Monastery Swiftspear's prowess trigger before or after that cascaded spell resolves?
results.text:
Monastery Swiftspear's prowess triggers immediately when you cast the noncreature spell via cascade, and that prowess trigger resolves before the cascaded spell does.

Here's the sequence: You cast Shardless Agent. Its cascade ability triggers and goes on the stack above Shardless Agent [702.85a, Shardless Agent ruling #1]. When the cascade ability resolves, you exile cards and may cast a nonland card with lesser mana value without paying its mana cost [608.2g]. When you cast that spell, Monastery Swiftspear's prowess triggers because you cast a noncreature spell [702.108a]. This prowess trigger is put on the stack on top of the spell that caused it [Monastery Swiftspear ruling #2]. Since no player receives priority during the resolution of the cascade ability [608.2g], the prowess trigger goes on the stack after the cascade ability finishes resolving completely. At that point, the stack has (from top to bottom): the prowess trigger, the cascaded spell, and then Shardless Agent. The prowess trigger will resolve first, giving Monastery Swiftspear +1/+1 until end of turn, and then the cascaded spell will resolve.

If the question assumes the cascaded spell is already on the stack and we are asking about the timing of the prowess trigger relative to its resolution, the answer is the same: the prowess trigger is put on the stack immediately when the spell is cast and will resolve before that spell.

results.question: My opponent's [Grizzly Bears] has 2 damage marked on it. Do state-based actions make it die before my [Lightning Bolt] resolves?
results.text:
No, state-based actions do not make your opponent's Grizzly Bears die before your Lightning Bolt resolves. The Grizzly Bears will be destroyed as a state-based action after Lightning Bolt finishes resolving.

Here's why: State-based actions are not checked during the resolution of a spell or ability [704.4]. When you cast Lightning Bolt targeting your opponent's Grizzly Bears, the spell goes on the stack and then resolves. During its resolution, Lightning Bolt deals 3 damage to the Grizzly Bears, marking that damage on it. At this point, the Grizzly Bears has a total of 5 damage marked on it (the existing 2 plus the new 3), and its toughness is 2. The condition for lethal damage is met (damage marked is greater than or equal to toughness), but state-based actions are not checked yet.

Only after Lightning Bolt has completely finished resolving does the game check state-based actions [704.3], [117.5]. At that check, seeing the Grizzly Bears has 5 damage marked and toughness 2, the state-based action in rule [704.5g] destroys it. The damage from Lightning Bolt does not itself destroy the creature; the state-based action does [120.5].

If the question's scenario were different and state-based actions were checked *before* you cast Lightning Bolt (for example, if you had priority with the Grizzly Bears already having 2 damage marked), then the Grizzly Bears would be destroyed immediately, and you could not target it with Lightning Bolt because it would be gone.

results.question: It's my upkeep. My [Phyrexian Arena]'s beginning-of-upkeep trigger and my opponent's own beginning-of-upkeep trigger both want to go on the stack. Who chooses the order, and when exactly do they trigger?
results.text:
Both Phyrexian Arena's ability and your opponent's beginning-of-upkeep ability trigger simultaneously at the beginning of the upkeep step. You, the active player, choose the order they are placed on the stack. The abilities are put onto the stack the next time a player would receive priority, which is immediately after the upkeep step begins and before you get priority.

According to rule 500.6, when the upkeep step begins, all abilities that trigger "at the beginning of" that step trigger. Rule 503.1a states that any abilities that triggered at the beginning of the upkeep are put onto the stack before the active player gets priority. Since multiple triggered abilities are waiting to be put on the stack, rule 603.3b explains the process: the abilities are placed on the stack in APNAP (Active Player, Nonactive Player) order. Specifically, rule 405.3 clarifies that when effects put two or more objects on the stack at the same time, those controlled by the active player are put on lowest (meaning you choose their order first), followed by each other player's objects. Therefore, you first choose the order for your Phyrexian Arena's trigger (and any other beginning-of-upkeep triggers you control), then your opponent chooses the order for their trigger(s). The stack is built with your chosen trigger(s) on the bottom and your opponent's chosen trigger(s) on top, so your opponent's ability will resolve first.

This answer assumes a two-player game. In a multiplayer game with more than two players, the nonactive players would put their triggers on the stack in turn order after the active player, following APNAP order.

results.question: I cast a sorcery with buyback and pay its buyback cost, then copy that spell with [Fork]. Once everything resolves, how many copies of the card end up back in my hand?
results.text:
You end up with exactly one copy of the card in your hand: the original sorcery card. The copy created by Fork does not return to your hand.

Here is the reasoning. You cast a sorcery with buyback and pay its buyback cost. According to rule 702.27a, paying the buyback cost is a decision made while casting the spell. The rule states that if the buyback cost was paid, the spell is put into its owner's hand instead of its owner's graveyard as it resolves. Therefore, when the original sorcery spell resolves, it will go to your hand.

You then copy that spell with Fork. Rule 707.10 explains that a copy of a spell copies all decisions made for the original spell, including additional costs like buyback. However, a copy of a spell is not cast (rule 707.10, Fork ruling #9). The copy is a spell on the stack with no associated card (rule 112.1a, Fork ruling #10). Fork ruling #8 directly addresses this interaction: "If you copy a spell for which Buyback has been paid, you get nothing back since the copied spell does not have a card to give you." This means the copy's buyback instruction cannot return a card to your hand because there is no card. When the copy resolves, as an instant or sorcery spell with no card, its final resolution step is to be put into its owner's graveyard (rule 608.2n). Since it has no owner's card associated with it, it simply ceases to exist as it leaves the stack.

Thus, only the original sorcery card returns to your hand via its own buyback ability. The copy does not produce a card for your hand.

results.question: I have a face-down manifested card that's really [Lightning Bolt]. It dies and I imprint it on [Mimic Vat]. Later I activate Mimic Vat's copy ability -- do I get a token?
results.text:
No, you do not get a token. When you activate Mimic Vat's ability, it attempts to create a token that's a copy of the exiled card. The exiled card is the Lightning Bolt, which is an instant card. An effect cannot create a token that is a copy of a nonpermanent card, so no token is created.

Here is the reasoning step by step. First, the face-down manifested Lightning Bolt dies. While manifested, it is a 2/2 colorless creature with no other characteristics. When it dies, it is put into its owner's graveyard. Mimic Vat's triggered ability triggers and you may choose to exile the Lightning Bolt card. If you do, the Lightning Bolt card is exiled. By default, exiled cards are face up, but the rules context does not specify that Mimic Vat exiles the card face down. Therefore, the Lightning Bolt card is exiled face up and is an instant card. Later, when you activate and resolve Mimic Vat's ability, it instructs you to "Create a token that's a copy of a card exiled with this artifact." The card exiled is the Lightning Bolt, an instant. Rule [111.12] states that if an effect instructs a player to create a token that is a copy of a nonexistent object, no token is created. A nonpermanent card (like an instant) is a nonexistent object for the purpose of creating a token copy. This is directly supported by [Mimic Vat ruling #0], which states that if Mimic Vat exiles a nonpermanent card (like an instant or sorcery from a manifested creature), you cannot create a token that's a copy of it, and no token is created. Therefore, no token is created.

Key definitions: A 'nonexistent object' for token creation includes cards that are not permanents (creature, artifact, enchantment, planeswalker, battle, or land). An instant card is a nonpermanent card. The face-down status of the permanent on the battlefield ([110.5d]) is irrelevant once the card is in the exile zone; in exile, the card's actual characteristics (in this case, an instant) are used ([406.3a], [708.12]).

results.question: My [Fiend Hunter]'s enters-the-battlefield ability is on the stack, about to exile a creature. I copy that ability with [Lithoform Engine] and target a second creature. Both get exiled. When Fiend Hunter later leaves the battlefield, do both come back?
results.text:
Yes, when Fiend Hunter later leaves the battlefield, both exiled creatures are returned to the battlefield under their owners' control.

Fiend Hunter has two linked abilities: its first ability exiles a creature, and its second ability returns "the exiled card" when Fiend Hunter leaves the battlefield. According to rule 607.1, these abilities are linked; the second refers only to creatures exiled by the first. Rule 607.2a further defines this as a type of linked ability where the second ability refers to cards exiled by an instruction in the first.

Lithoform Engine ruling #4 directly addresses this interaction. It states that if an ability is linked to a second ability, copies of that first ability are also linked to that second ability. If the second ability refers to "the exiled card," it refers to all cards exiled by the first ability and the copy. Therefore, when you copy Fiend Hunter's enters-the-battlefield ability with Lithoform Engine, both the original and the copy are linked to Fiend Hunter's leaves-the-battlefield ability. When Fiend Hunter leaves the battlefield, its second ability triggers and returns both creatures that were exiled by the linked abilities.

results.question: My own [Banishing Light] has an opponent's creature exiled. On my opponent's turn I cast [Teferi's Protection], phasing out my Banishing Light. Does the exiled creature return to the battlefield?
results.text:
No, the exiled creature does not return to the battlefield when Banishing Light phases out. The creature remains exiled.

Teferi's Protection causes all permanents you control, including Banishing Light, to phase out. Phasing out is not a zone change; Banishing Light remains on the battlefield but is treated as though it doesn't exist [702.26d]. The one-shot effect created by Banishing Light's triggered ability exiles the target permanent "until this enchantment leaves the battlefield." According to the specific ruling for Teferi's Protection, any one-shot effects waiting "until [this] leaves the battlefield," such as that of Banishing Light, won't happen when a permanent phases out [Teferi's Protection ruling #21]. Therefore, the condition for the creature to return (Banishing Light leaving the battlefield) is not met by phasing out. The effect that would cause the creature to phase in, as described in rules for "until" effects [610.4, 610.4a], is not created because the triggering event (Banishing Light leaving the battlefield) did not occur. The creature stays in exile. Additionally, any Auras attached to Banishing Light (though not relevant here) would phase out indirectly along with it [702.26g] and would phase in with it later.

results.question: I cast [Emrakul, the Promised End]. In response to its cast trigger, my opponent tries to [Counterspell] it. Can they even target it given protection from instants, and if it's countered, do I still control their next turn?
results.text:
Yes, your opponent can target Emrakul, the Promised End with Counterspell, and if Emrakul, the Promised End is countered, you will still control that opponent's next turn.

Emrakul, the Promised End's protection from instants is a static ability that only applies while Emrakul, the Promised End is on the battlefield [Emrakul, the Promised End ruling #2]. While Emrakul, the Promised End is on the stack, it is a spell, not a permanent, so protection from instants does not apply and does not prevent it from being targeted by Counterspell [Emrakul, the Promised End ruling #2]. Therefore, your opponent can legally choose Emrakul, the Promised End as the target for Counterspell [601.2c].

When you cast Emrakul, the Promised End, its triggered ability ('When you cast this spell...') triggers and is put on the stack on top of Emrakul, the Promised End [603.1a, 117.2a]. Your opponent casts Counterspell 'in response to' this triggered ability, meaning Counterspell goes on the stack above the triggered ability [117.7]. Counterspell will resolve first. If Counterspell resolves and counters Emrakul, the Promised End, Emrakul, the Promised End is put into its owner's graveyard. However, the triggered ability from casting Emrakul, the Promised End is a separate object on the stack and is not countered by Counterspell (Counterspell only counters the spell, not abilities) [113.9]. After Counterspell resolves, the triggered ability remains on the stack and will resolve normally, allowing you to gain control of the target opponent during their next turn. A spell or ability on the stack cannot target itself [115.5], but this is not relevant here as Counterspell is targeting Emrakul, the Promised End, not the triggered ability.

This answer assumes a standard two-player game. In a Grand Melee game with multiple stacks, the targeting and stack order rules are more complex [807.5b], but the core principle that protection doesn't apply on the stack remains.

results.question: My cascade spell exiles cards until it hits [Valki, God of Lies], whose back face is the seven-mana planeswalker Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor. Is that a legal cascade hit, and can I cast the Tibalt side for free?
results.text:
Yes, Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor is a legal cascade hit, and you may cast the Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor side for free. When the cascade ability exiles Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor, you may choose to cast either face, as long as the resulting spell's mana value is less than the cascading spell's mana value. Since you are casting it for free via cascade, you choose which face to cast as part of the casting process. The mana value of Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor is 2, which is less than the cascading spell's mana value, so it qualifies. You may choose to cast the Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor side (mana value 7) because cascade only checks the mana value of the card in exile (which is 2) and the resulting spell's mana value (which would be 7). Since 7 is less than the cascading spell's mana value (which must be greater than 7 for this to be true), casting Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor is allowed.

This is grounded in the cascade rule [702.85a], which exiles a nonland card and checks if its mana value is less than the cascading spell's. For double-faced cards, the mana value is calculated using the mana cost of the front face [712.8c], which for Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor is 2. Rule [712.11c] states that only the face that will be face up on the stack is evaluated to determine if it can be cast. When casting from exile via cascade, you are allowed to look at the card [406.3b, 601.3f] and, per the card's specific ruling [Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor ruling #16], you may cast a modal double-faced card with any face that fits the criteria of the effect. The cascade effect allows you to cast the exiled card without paying its mana cost if the resulting spell's mana value is less than the cascading spell's. Therefore, you may choose to cast the Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor side, and its mana value (7) is checked as the 'resulting spell's mana value' against the cascading spell's mana value.
citations: Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor ruling #16

results.question: I cast [Emrakul, the Promised End]. With its cast trigger on the stack, I copy that trigger with [Lithoform Engine]. Then I untap Lithoform Engine with [Voltaic Key] and use it again to copy [Emrakul, the Promised End] itself as a permanent spell. How many of my opponent's turns do I control, do I get a second Emrakul, and does copying the Emrakul spell give me another control-a-turn trigger?
results.text:
You will control one of your opponent's turns, and you will get a second Emrakul, the Promised End token, but copying the Emrakul, the Promised End spell does not give you another control-a-turn trigger.

First, copying the cast trigger of Emrakul, the Promised End with Lithoform Engine's first ability puts a copy of that triggered ability on the stack [707.10]. The copy of the ability is not cast, so it does not trigger abilities that trigger when a spell is cast [Lithoform Engine ruling #6]. The copy of the ability will resolve and create its own effect to control a target opponent's next turn. However, if both the original Emrakul, the Promised End trigger and the copy target the same opponent, the effects overwrite each other, and the last one created (which will be the copy if you put it on the stack last) is the one that works [Emrakul, the Promised End ruling #14]. Therefore, you will ultimately control only one of that opponent's turns.

Second, copying the Emrakul, the Promised End permanent spell with Lithoform Engine's third ability puts a copy of that spell on the stack [707.10]. When that copy resolves, it becomes a token that is a copy of Emrakul, the Promised End [111.13]. So you get a second Emrakul, the Promised End token.

Third, copying the Emrakul, the Promised End spell does not trigger its cast ability. A copy of a spell is put onto the stack; it is not cast [707.10b]. The triggered ability of Emrakul, the Promised End triggers when you cast it, not when a copy of it is put onto the stack. Therefore, copying the spell does not give you another control-a-turn trigger.

Assumptions: This answer assumes a two-player game. In a multiplayer game, if you target different opponents with the original and copied triggers, you would control each of those opponents' next turns. The provided rules do not specify multiplayer turn order, so the answer for more than two players would depend on those rules.

results.question: I've imprinted a creature on [Mimic Vat] and activate its ability to make a token copy. While that ability is on the stack, I copy it with [Lithoform Engine]. Do I get two tokens?
results.text:
Yes, you get two tokens. When you copy Mimic Vat's activated ability with Lithoform Engine, you put a copy of that ability onto the stack. Both the original ability and the copy will resolve independently. As long as a card is exiled with Mimic Vat when each ability resolves, each will create a token that's a copy of that card, and each token gains haste and will be exiled at the beginning of the next end step.

This works because copying an ability means putting a copy of it onto the stack; the copy is itself an ability [707.10, 707.10b]. Lithoform Engine's first ability targets an activated ability on the stack and creates another instance of that ability [Lithoform Engine ruling #3]. Each instance of Mimic Vat's ability, when it resolves, checks whether a card is exiled with Mimic Vat at that moment. If a card is exiled, it creates a token copy [Mimic Vat ruling #6]. Since you imprinted a creature, there is a card exiled, so both the original and the copied ability will create a token.

Note: The copy of the ability has the same source as the original ability [707.10b], which is Mimic Vat. Both abilities refer to "a card exiled with this artifact," meaning Mimic Vat. At the time each resolves, you look at the cards currently exiled with Mimic Vat and choose one to copy (if multiple are exiled) [Mimic Vat ruling #1]. In your scenario, with only one card exiled, both tokens will be copies of that same card.

results.question: An opponent controls an untapped [Trinisphere], and I have a permanent that makes my green spells cost {1} less. I want to cast [Awaken the Woods] for value. If I cast it with X=0, what does it cost and what do I get, and what X should I actually choose?
results.text:
If you cast Awaken the Woods with X=0 while an opponent controls an untapped Trinisphere and you have a permanent that makes your green spells cost {1} less, the total cost is {G}{G} and you get zero tokens. To get any tokens, you must choose X=1 or greater, and the total cost will be at least {2}{G}{G}.

Here's the reasoning: Awaken the Woods has a mana cost of {X}{G}{G}. When you cast it, you first choose a value for X. With X=0, the mana cost is {0}{G}{G}, which is {G}{G}. Your cost reduction effect makes your green spells cost {1} less. According to rule 118.7a, effects that reduce a cost by an amount of generic mana affect only the generic mana component. Since the mana cost {G}{G} has a generic mana component of {0}, the reduction has nothing to reduce. The total cost before Trinisphere is still {G}{G}. Trinisphere's effect then applies because the mana component of the cost ({G}{G}) is less than three mana. Trinisphere makes the spell cost three mana to cast. The cost becomes three mana, which must include the colored mana requirements. You must pay {G}{G} for the two green mana symbols, and you need one additional mana of any color or colorless to reach three total mana. Therefore, the total cost is {G}{G} plus one generic mana, which can be written as {1}{G}{G}. You pay this cost, and since X=0, you create zero 1/1 green Forest Dryad land creature tokens.

To get tokens, you must choose X=1 or more. If you choose X=1, the mana cost is {1}{G}{G}. Your cost reduction reduces the generic mana component by {1}, making it {0}{G}{G}. Trinisphere then checks the mana component, which is now {G}{G} (two mana), and increases it to three mana. The cost becomes {1}{G}{G} again. You would pay {1}{G}{G} and create one token. For any X >= 1, the cost reduction will first reduce the generic mana component (X) by 1, and then Trinisphere will ensure the total mana paid is at least three. The minimum cost to get at least one token is {2}{G}{G} (achieved with X=1, reduced to X=0 by the reduction, then increased to three total mana by Trinisphere).

This answer is for a two-player game. In a multiplayer game with more than one opponent, the presence of Trinisphere controlled by any opponent would have the same effect.

results.question: [Grist, the Hunger Tide] is in my graveyard. Can I return it with [Animate Dead], and what happens?
results.text:
Yes, you can return Grist, the Hunger Tide from your graveyard to the battlefield with Animate Dead. When Animate Dead's triggered ability resolves, Grist, the Hunger Tide will be put onto the battlefield as a creature, but Animate Dead will fail to attach to it and be put into the graveyard, causing you to sacrifice Grist, the Hunger Tide.

Here is the sequence: Animate Dead is an Aura that can target a creature card in a graveyard. While Grist, the Hunger Tide is in your graveyard, its first ability makes it a creature card in addition to its other types, so it is a legal target for Animate Dead [Grist, the Hunger Tide ruling #1]. You cast Animate Dead targeting Grist, the Hunger Tide. When Animate Dead enters the battlefield, its triggered ability goes on the stack. When that ability resolves, it returns the targeted Grist, the Hunger Tide card to the battlefield under your control [Animate Dead ruling #1]. However, as soon as Grist, the Hunger Tide enters the battlefield, it is no longer a creature; it is just a planeswalker [Grist, the Hunger Tide ruling #1]. Animate Dead's ability tries to attach it to the returned permanent, but Animate Dead has gained "enchant creature" and the returned Grist, the Hunger Tide is not a creature. Therefore, Animate Dead cannot legally enchant it [Animate Dead ruling #4]. As a state-based action, Animate Dead is put into its owner's graveyard. When Animate Dead leaves the battlefield, its delayed triggered ability triggers, and when that ability resolves, the controller of the creature it was attached to (you) sacrifices that permanent. Since Grist, the Hunger Tide was the creature put onto the battlefield with Animate Dead, you must sacrifice Grist, the Hunger Tide.

If the timing of Animate Dead's triggered ability resolution is such that Grist, the Hunger Tide is somehow not on the battlefield when the ability tries to return it (for example, if it was removed from the graveyard in response), then the ability does nothing [Animate Dead ruling #0]. The provided scenario assumes Grist, the Hunger Tide is in the graveyard as the ability resolves.

results.question: My commander [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave] has four +1/+1 counters on it. It dies, I move it to the command zone, then recast it. Does it keep the counters, and does [Doubling Season] double them as it re-enters?
results.text:
Skullbriar, the Walking Grave keeps its four +1/+1 counters when it moves to the command zone and when it is recast, and Doubling Season does not double those counters as it re-enters the battlefield.

Skullbriar, the Walking Grave's ability states that counters remain on it as it moves to any zone other than a player's hand or library. This includes moving to the command zone via the replacement effect in rule 903.9b. Therefore, when Skullbriar, the Walking Grave dies and its owner chooses to put it into the command zone, it retains all four +1/+1 counters. When Skullbriar, the Walking Grave is later cast from the command zone and enters the battlefield, it is a new object due to rule 400.7, but its own ability causes it to retain the counters from its previous existence as an exception to that rule.

Doubling Season's effect applies when an effect would put one or more counters on a permanent you control. However, the counters Skullbriar, the Walking Grave retains are not being 'put' on it by an effect as it enters the battlefield; they are simply remaining on it due to its own static ability. A ruling for Skullbriar, the Walking Grave explicitly states these counters aren't 'placed,' so effects like Doubling Season's won't affect them. Therefore, Doubling Season does not double the number of counters Skullbriar, the Walking Grave has when it re-enters the battlefield; it enters with the same four +1/+1 counters it had in the command zone.

results.question: I cast [Final Fortune] to take an extra turn. During that extra turn I use [Sundial of the Infinite] to end the turn before the end step. Do I still lose the game?
results.text: No, you do not lose the game. When you activate Sundial of the Infinite's ability during your extra turn, it ends the turn and skips straight to the cleanup step, which includes skipping the end step. Since the end step is skipped, the triggered ability from Final Fortune that says "At the beginning of that turn's end step, you lose the game" does not trigger at all that turn. According to the ruling for Final Fortune, if you skip the extra turn, you do not lose the game; the same principle applies when you skip the end step of that extra turn, preventing the lose-the-game trigger from ever occurring. The process of ending the turn exiles all spells and abilities on the stack, ends the current phase/step, and skips to the cleanup step, bypassing the end step entirely [724.1d]. Because the end step is skipped, "at the beginning of the end step" triggered abilities do not trigger [724.1e]. Since the Final Fortune's lose-the-game ability never triggers, you do not lose the game.

results.question: I cast [Clone]. When and how do I choose what it copies, and can my opponent respond to that choice?
results.text:
You choose which creature Clone copies as part of the process of casting Clone, specifically when you are announcing the spell's targets and other choices. Your opponent cannot respond to that specific choice because it is made during the casting process before the spell is put on the stack and players receive priority. The choice is not a target, so it can be any creature on the battlefield, even one with shroud or hexproof.

According to rule 601.2c, when casting a spell, a player announces choices for targets. Rule 601.5 clarifies that while announcing these choices, a player may consider other choices to be made later in the spellcasting process. Clone's ability is a choice made as you are casting it, not a target (as confirmed by Clone ruling #0). Therefore, you decide which creature Clone will copy as you are proposing the spell, before moving to paying costs. Once you finish casting Clone and it is on the stack, players get priority and your opponent can respond to the Clone spell itself, but the choice of what to copy has already been made and cannot be changed in response.

If the timing of events in the question is ambiguous, assuming you mean the normal sequence of casting a spell, the answer is as above. If, instead, the question is about responding to the moment Clone's enters-the-battlefield ability is applied (which is a replacement effect), the answer changes: the choice for that replacement effect is made as Clone is entering the battlefield, which is after the spell has resolved and no player has priority, so opponents also cannot respond to that choice.

results.question: I activate my [Flooded Strand]'s ability, then activate [Gogo, Master of Mimicry] with X=2 to copy it twice. How many lands do I get from that one Flooded Strand?
results.text:
You will get a total of three lands onto the battlefield: one from the original Flooded Strand ability and two from the copies created by Gogo, Master of Mimicry.

Gogo, Master of Mimicry's ability copies the targeted activated ability on the stack [Gogo, Master of Mimicry ruling #6]. Each copy is a separate instance of the ability that will resolve independently [707.10]. The original Flooded Strand ability instructs you to search your library for a Plains or Island card and put it onto the battlefield. Each copy of that ability will also instruct you to search your library for a Plains or Island card and put it onto the battlefield. However, rule 701.23h states that if an effect instructs a player to search a library for one or more cards more than once before instructing that player to shuffle that library, it is treated as a single instruction to search for all those cards. Therefore, when the original ability and the two copies resolve, you will perform one combined search of your library for up to three Plains and/or Island cards (one for each ability), put all of them onto the battlefield, and then shuffle your library once.

Citations: [701.23h], [707.10], [Gogo, Master of Mimicry ruling #6], [Gogo, Master of Mimicry ruling #9].
